did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with a challenging question: If a person seeks help, whom should they turn to? It presents turning to God as one possibility.
The verse emphasizes that human beings are born to trouble and compares them to the “sons of Resheph” who fly upward—a poetic description of a human existence filled with toil and movement.
The speaker declares that instead of relying on his own strength, he will turn to God and present his case to Him.
God’s greatness is described as beyond full comprehension: He does wonders that cannot be counted.
Rain is presented in the chapter as an expression of God’s activity, watering both the face of the earth and the fields and open places.
One description of God’s action is the reversal of fortunes: He lifts up the lowly and brings deliverance to the afflicted and oppressed.
The chapter describes God as frustrating the schemes of the crafty, so that their plans do not succeed or benefit them.
The verse presents accepting God’s discipline as a blessing and warns against rejecting His correction or discipline.
God is described as one who wounds but also bandages, who strikes but also heals—emphasizing His ability to bring both harm and restoration.
The expression “in six troubles... and in seven” poetically portrays repeated and extensive protection from various troubles, including famine, war, plunder, and wild animals.
